title: How good does a cloth simulator have to be before the laundry-robot hanger it designs is the right one?
lede: research programme: how much cloth-simulator fidelity and fabric data a laundry-robot hanger design loop needs before its choice holds on a validated solver; milestone 1, on four fabrics with published KES-FB bending rigidity and weight, finds the 2D chain and 3D sheet agree on every decision (wood-shaped hanger, arm 1 cm wider than the half shoulder) but agree to 0.004 cm because on a deep arm they are one model, and on a 3 cm arm the solver error (0.05 to 0.11 cm) is as large as the margin that picks the width (0.08 to 0.13 cm); milestone 1b solves the 3 cm arm to convergence and its best width moves to +1.5 cm on all four fabrics, against +1.0 cm in the 2D chain, a disagreement the 3000-iteration cap hid by flattering narrow arms; milestone 2a builds a simulated Cusick drape test on the 3D sheet: it orders the fabrics by bending length, but unmeasured stretch stiffness moves the drape coefficient 0.15 to 0.23 and, stiffened, every fabric drapes alike at about 0.77 (the spring grid locks), so drape cannot calibrate bending rigidity on this tier; milestone 1c reruns the 3 cm arm across stretch stiffness and mesh: the mesh leaves the width choice alone, but EA moves it from +2.0 to +2.5 cm at 40 N/m to +0.5 to +1.0 cm at 800 N/m while the 2D chain stays near +1.0 cm, so the tier disagreement changes sign with an unmeasured fabric property; milestone 2b refines the drape test's grid to 2.5 mm: the stiff suiting converges but the soft jersey does not above 150 N/m, and swapping springs shows most of the leftover stretch dependence is the shear spring the model ties to EA, a stiffness the same KES table measures (G = 26 to 89 N/m)
summary: An open research programme on designing a laundry robot's hangers by cloth simulation: how much simulator fidelity and how much measured fabric data the design loop needs before the hanger it picks is still the best one on a validated, calibrated solver, and whether cheap models can certify that. The proposal reviews 19 works (cloth solvers, cloth parameter fitting, the cloth sim-to-real gap, multi-fidelity and robust design), states four falsifiable hypotheses and targets IEEE RA-L. Milestone 1 scores three stock hangers and five arm widths on four fabrics whose bending rigidity (0.0066 to 0.125 gf·cm²/cm) and weight are published KES-FB measurements, in three model tiers (2D chain, 3D sheet on a slab arm, 3D sheet on a 3 cm half-depth arm scored on the whole sheet). Every tier picks the wood-shaped hanger (0.38 to 0.47 cm RMS from the worn shape on the slab, against 3.1 to 3.4 cm for wire and plastic) and an arm 1 cm wider than the half shoulder on every fabric; the only ranking disagreement is a tie for second place. But on a deep arm the 2D and 3D errors differ by at most 0.004 cm, so their agreement is no test of fidelity, and on the 3 cm arm doubling the solver iterations moves the error by 0.05 to 0.11 cm, the same size as the 0.08 to 0.13 cm margin that decides the width. Milestone 1b solves those 3 cm-arm cases to convergence (12,000 to 24,000 iterations, error change under 0.002 cm per 3000). The best width moves to +1.5 cm on all four fabrics (on the 1 cm grid, +2 on fabric D), while the 2D chain stays sharply at +1.0 cm. The 3000-iteration bias depends on the width (+0.22 cm at −1 cm, −0.07 cm at +3 cm), so stopping early favoured narrow arms and made the tiers look as if they agreed. Simulation only: stretch stiffness (150 N/m) is assumed, garments are one size-M strip, there is no friction and no validated solver yet. Milestone 2a builds a simulated Cusick drape test (30 cm specimen on an 18 cm disc) on the same sheet, made isotropic in bending, and solves 140 cases to a drape-coefficient stopping rule. The drape coefficient orders the four fabrics by bending length (0.19, 0.21, 0.32, 0.45) with seed noise under 0.01, but the unmeasured stretch stiffness moves it by 0.15 to 0.23 (EA 40 against 800 N/m), shear by 0.08 to 0.11 and the mesh by up to 0.05; post hoc, stiffening the springs to 12,800 N/m lifts every fabric to about 0.77, so two fabrics with 19-fold different bending rigidity drape alike. That is membrane locking of the square spring grid: on this tier a measured drape coefficient cannot pin bending rigidity, so drape calibration moves to the validated top tier, whose first acceptance test is this one. No measured drape table could be reached this session. Milestone 1c reruns the converged 3 cm arm on fabrics A and D at EA 40, 150 and 800 N/m and two mesh changes (70 cases, all converged, predictions committed first): the mesh keeps the +1.5 cm choice, but the 3D sheet's best width goes from +2.0 to +2.5 cm at EA 40 to +0.5 to +1.0 cm at EA 800, while the 2D chain stays at +1.0 cm (+1.5 for fabric D at EA 40). The 3D-against-2D disagreement therefore runs from +1.0 to −0.5 cm with a stretch stiffness the KES-FB2 table does not give: on a shallow arm, bending rigidity and weight do not pick the hanger on this tier, and measured tensile data is a precondition for calibration. Milestone 2b refines the drape test's spring grid from 7.5 to 2.5 mm (26 cases, predictions committed first). The stiff suiting converges to about 0.01, but the soft jersey does not at EA 800 N/m and up (0.70 to 0.37 at EA 3200, still falling), and the overhang barely compresses at any EA (under 0.15%). A post hoc swap shows the sheet's shear spring, tied to EA at 0.1, carries most of the leftover dependence: on the suiting at 2.5 mm, shear alone (80 to 320 N/m) raises DC by 0.046 and stretch alone (800 to 3200 N/m) by 0.027; on the jersey, 0.139 against 0.013. Shear rigidity is measured in the same KES table as B and W (G = 0.47 to 1.58 gf/cm/deg, 26 to 89 N/m per radian), so it can now be set from data; the shallow-arm width shift of milestone 1c uses the same coupling and is the next thing to recheck.
